lines.text: Finding the address. Every time you open a website, your computer has to answer one question first. What number belongs to this name?
You typed eleven characters, and pressed Enter. Your computer now has about two hundred milliseconds to turn a name into a number.
The name is example dot com. Your computer cannot use it. Computers find each other by number. So the first job is to translate the name into one.
Your computer doesn't know the number. So it asks. Not the whole internet, just one machine. A D N S resolver. Usually your internet provider runs it.

The resolver probably doesn't know either. So it goes looking. First, a root server, which knows who runs dot com. Then the dot com server, which knows who runs example dot com. Then the registrar, which finally knows the address.
Three questions. Three round trips across the network. And this time, a real answer. Ninety three. One eighty four. Two sixteen. Thirty four.
But here is what makes everything after this feel fast. The answer gets remembered. Your computer keeps it. Your resolver keeps it. For minutes, sometimes hours, that name resolves instantly.
We are twenty percent through the budget. Forty milliseconds gone. Three round trips. And we have not opened a single connection.
That was one step out of five. We haven't connected. We haven't proved it's safe. We haven't even asked for the page.
Next, we open the connection. Three packets. One round trip.
